```{python}
#| label: setup
import re
import sys
from pathlib import Path

sys.path.insert(0, str(Path.cwd()))
from IPython.display import Markdown, display

import figures as F
import paperdata as D
from paperdata import (bn, count, fy, gbp, listing, md_table, num, ordinal, pct, points, pm, rate, wk, words)

FINAL, SWITCH = D.FINAL, D.SWITCH
MID = D.DIST_YEARS[0]  # the first household-table year, five rises after the switch
FLOOR = D.FLOOR_TEXT
TENTH = num(100 * 10 ** -D.RATE_DECIMALS, 1)  # the inputs' published precision, in points
MAX_AGE = num(D.R["coverage"]["datasets"]["primary"]["max_age"], 0)
H = D.EV["backtest"]["horizon_years"]  # rises after each backtest origin
TLL, BPL = D.LABELS["triple_lock"], D.LABELS["burnham_2030"]
DWP_TEXT = (D.ROOT / D.DWP["file"]).read_text()


def lower1(t):
    return t[0].lower() + t[1:]


# The headline figures.
g_final, n_final = D.est("gross", FINAL), D.est("net", FINAL)
lose_final = D.est("households_losing_pct", FINAL)
central = D.path("central")
c_final = D.row(central, FINAL)
gap = D.EV["gap_by_calibration"][D.PRIMARY]
dwp_nominal = D.DWP["saving_bn"][str(FINAL)]["nominal"]
dwp_real = D.DWP["saving_bn"][str(FINAL)]["real_2025_26_prices"]
obr_premium, _ = D.obr_premium_text()
prem = D.premium()
sens = D.EV["sensitivities"]
sens_g = [v["gross"][str(FINAL)]["mean"] for v in sens.values()]
first_group = next(g for g in D.history_groups() if g["changes"])
last_hist = D.HISTORY["model_years"][-1]
past_weekly = first_group["model"]["counterfactual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(last_hist)]
actual_weekly = first_group["model"]["actual_weekly"]["new_state_pension"][str(last_hist)]
past_saving = first_group["model"]["saving_bn"][str(last_hist)]
rnd = D.path("random")
p50, p90 = D.path("monthly_p50"), D.path("monthly_p90")
priv_share = D.borne_share(D.examples(rnd)["private_pension"], FINAL)
# The pensioner on the guarantee: Pension Credit replaces the after-tax loss exactly, and the whole of the small gain
# is council tax reduction, which the regulations would leave unchanged (@sec-step4).
g_owner = D.examples(rnd)["owner"]
g_cut = -D.ex_change(g_owner, "state_pension", FINAL)
g_gain = D.ex_change(g_owner, "net_income", FINAL)
assert abs(D.ex_change(g_owner, "pension_credit", FINAL) - (g_cut + D.ex_change(g_owner, "income_tax", FINAL))) < 0.05
assert g_gain > 0.5 and abs(g_gain - D.ex_change(g_owner, "council_tax_reduction", FINAL)) < 0.05
dwp_quote = re.search(r"In any given year it will go up by.*?that value", DWP_TEXT).group(0)
```

## Summary {.unnumbered}

::: {.summary-box}
On 29 September 2026 the Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, said he would keep the State Pension triple lock until 2030 and then "adjust" it, and that the pension "will hold its value relative to earnings over time" [@bbc_live2026]. DWP describes the change: from April `{python} SWITCH` the pension will keep the record high value relative to earnings it reaches under the triple lock, and "`{python} dwp_quote`" [@dwp_uprating2026]. We read inflation as September CPI, earnings as May–July average weekly earnings, and the record value as the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level, and compare this Burnham plan with the triple lock to `{python} fy(FINAL)` using PolicyEngine UK. Every fiscal and household figure in this paper is a full model run of the whole survey population, or of an example household, under each rule; nothing is scaled or extrapolated from another run.

The plan keeps the triple lock's floor and its protection against prices, but drops its ratchet. It saves money only after years in which the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR` exceeds earnings growth: the triple lock keeps that extra rise for good, while the plan waits for earnings to catch up. On the OBR's central forecast earnings lead in almost every year after the switch, so the plan saves `{python} bn(c_final["gross"])` in State Pension spending in `{python} fy(FINAL)` (`{python} bn(c_final["net"])` net of tax and benefits). The average saving across possible paths is far larger than the saving on the average path, because the saving grows only when the lead passes between prices and earnings, which the smooth central path hardly does. We simulate `{python} count(D.EV["draws"]["n"])` paths of prices and earnings, shifted so that their average in each calendar year equals the OBR's forecast to 2030 and its long-term projection after, and run `{python} count(D.n_unique())` of them in full (and one more to confirm that the paths on which the rules never differ save nothing). The expected saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is `{python} bn(g_final["mean"])` in State Pension spending (Monte Carlo standard error `{python} bn(g_final["se"])`), or `{python} bn(n_final["mean"])` (standard error `{python} bn(n_final["se"])`) once income tax, Pension Credit and other benefits respond. The standard error measures only the sampling of paths: other calibrations of the same model, which did worse in our backtest, give `{python} bn(min(sens_g), 1)` to `{python} bn(max(sens_g), 1)` gross, the highest resting on few effective runs (@sec-calibration). DWP costs the plan at £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn that year, on one path through its dynamic model, for Great Britain.

Under the plan about `{python} pct(lose_final["mean"], 0)` of households have a lower income in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. In law a pensioner whose income after tax is at the Pension Credit guarantee comes out even, because extra Pension Credit and a lower tax bill replace the lost pension. In the model such a pensioner on the random path of @sec-step4 comes out `{python} gbp(g_gain, 2)` a year ahead on a `{python} gbp(g_cut, 2)` pension cut in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, because policyengine-uk also raises their council tax reduction, which the regulations would leave unchanged: that gain is a gap in the model, not part of the plan. A pensioner with a `{python} gbp(D.examples(rnd)["private_pension"]["meta"]["private_pension"])` private pension bears `{python} pct(100 * priv_share, 0)` of the cut.
:::

## Introduction

The triple lock has raised the basic State Pension each April since 2011, and the new State Pension since it began in 2016, by the highest of CPI inflation, earnings growth and `{python} FLOOR`. Because it takes the highest of the three each year, it works as a ratchet: a year in which prices or the floor run ahead of earnings raises the pension for good, and later rises build on the higher level. The Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) assumes in its long-term projections that the triple lock raises the pension by `{python} obr_premium` percentage points a year more than earnings [@obr_lted2026].

The Prime Minister set out a change from April 2030 in his speech to Labour's conference on 29 September 2026. As the BBC reported it, he said he would "adjust" the triple lock, that the pension would rise every year at least by inflation or `{python} FLOOR`, and that "it will hold its value relative to earnings over time" [@bbc_live2026]. DWP's State Pension uprating analysis, published the same day, says the pension will reach "a record high relative to earnings over the coming three years" and from April 2030 will retain "that record high value relative to earnings": "`{python} dwp_quote`" [@dwp_uprating2026]. DWP does not state the measures of inflation and earnings or the base year. We take the triple lock's own measures, September CPI and May–July average weekly earnings, and the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level as the base, and call the result the Burnham plan.

This paper builds the answer up in six steps, the same six the accompanying dashboard follows. We start with how the triple lock works and what the plan would have paid had it started earlier (@sec-step1); run both rules on the OBR's central forecast (@sec-step2); then on another path of prices and earnings (@sec-step3); follow example pensioners along that path (@sec-step4) and the whole population (@sec-step5); and finally average over many paths to get the expected saving (@sec-step6). @sec-method describes the method and its limitations, and @sec-appendix-backtest tests the forecast distributions behind the paths.

Every fiscal and household figure is a full run of PolicyEngine UK (policyengine `{python} D.BUNDLE["policyengine_version"]`, policyengine-uk `{python} D.BUNDLE["model_version"]`) [@policyengine_py; @policyengine_uk] on the Enhanced Family Resources Survey (FRS) for `{python} fy(2024)` (`{python} D.BUNDLE["certified_data_build_id"]`, `{python} count(D.R["coverage"]["datasets"]["primary"]["records"]["households"])` household records). A second, larger PolicyEngine dataset, Microcosm (`{python} D.EV["datasets"]["sensitivity"]`, `{python} count(D.R["coverage"]["datasets"]["sensitivity"]["records"]["households"])` household records, about `{python} words(round(D.R["coverage"]["datasets"]["sensitivity"]["records"]["households"] / D.R["coverage"]["datasets"]["primary"]["records"]["households"]))` times as many), is a sensitivity. A path's CPI and earnings growth enter the model's economic assumptions before the data load, so benefit rates, CPI-indexed tax thresholds and earnings follow it; the State Pension flat rates are then set from each rule. Weekly amounts, rates and the spread of the pension gap across paths are rule arithmetic and are labelled as such. All money is in cash terms. Fiscal years are named by their first year in figures ("`{python} FINAL`" is `{python} fy(FINAL)`).

## How the triple lock works {#sec-step1}

```{python}
rec = D.tl_record()
first, last = rec[0], rec[-1]
counts = {k: sum(r["binding"] == k for r in rec) for k in ("cpi", "earnings", "floor")}
idx = last["index"]
rise = {k: 100 * (idx[k] - 1) for k in idx}
above_earn = 100 * (idx["triple_lock"] / idx["earnings"] - 1)
paid_diff = [r for r in rec if round(r["paid"] * 1000) != round(r["rate"] * 1000)]
susp_year = D.HISTORY["suspended_earnings_year"]
susp = next(r for r in rec if r["year"] == susp_year)
```

### The rule and its inputs

Each April the full basic and new State Pension rise by the highest of three figures: the CPI 12-month rate for the previous September [@ons_d7g7]; growth in average weekly earnings (AWE), whole-economy total pay, in May to July of the previous year over the same months a year earlier [@ons_kac3]; and `{python} FLOOR`. The law requires the basic and new State Pension to rise at least in line with earnings [@ssaa1992_s150a]; the prices leg and the floor are policy on top. ONS publishes both inputs to `{python} TENTH` point, and the rules here take them at that precision, so the triple lock's rate is exactly the larger input or the floor. Only the flat-rate pensions are triple-locked. The additional State Pension rises with September CPI under both rules here, as DWP's analysis assumes for the parts of the pre-2016 pension that the triple lock does not cover [@dwp_uprating2026].

### The triple lock since 2011

@fig-history and @tbl-history replay the rule on the published inputs for each April from `{python} first["year"]` to `{python} last["year"]`, using the latest ONS figures. CPI set the rise `{python} words(counts["cpi"])` times, earnings `{python} words(counts["earnings"])` times and the floor `{python} words(counts["floor"])` times. Over those `{python} len(rec)` rises the triple lock raised the pension by `{python} pct(rise["triple_lock"], 0)` in all, against `{python} pct(rise["earnings"], 0)` for earnings alone, `{python} pct(rise["cpi"], 0)` for prices alone and `{python} pct(rise["floor"], 0)` for `{python} FLOOR` a year. The ratchet leaves the pension `{python} pct(above_earn, 1)` above where an earnings link alone would have taken it.

In April `{python} susp_year` the law suspended the earnings leg, whose May–July input was `{python} rate(susp["earnings"])`, so that April's rise was CPI (`{python} rate(susp["cpi"])`) [@ssuba2021]; the replay does the same, though the earnings-alone line uses the published figure. The replay differs from the rise actually paid in `{python} len(paid_diff)` of `{python} len(rec)` years (`{python} listing([f'April {r["year"]}: paid {rate(r["paid"])}, rule {rate(r["rate"])}' for r in paid_diff], sep="; ")`), because the rises paid used the figures first published, and April `{python} first["year"]`'s rise, set by that year's up-rating order, was larger than the rule gives [@uprating2011].

### The Burnham plan's rule

The Burnham plan follows the triple lock to April `{python} SWITCH - 1`. DWP's description is that from then on "`{python} dwp_quote`", where the value is the pension's record high relative to earnings [@dwp_uprating2026]. We write this as follows. From April `{python} SWITCH` let $L_t$ be the pension's level and $A_t$ an earnings path that starts at the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level and grows with May–July earnings, $A_t = A_{t-1}(1 + e_{t-1})$. Then

$$L_t = \max\bigl(L_{t-1}\,(1 + \max(c_{t-1}, f)),\; A_t\bigr),$$

where $c$ is September CPI, $e$ is May–July earnings growth and $f$ is the `{python} FLOOR` floor. The pension never rises by less than the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR`, and never falls below its earnings path. The top-up to the earnings path is rounded up to `{python} TENTH` point, so rounding never leaves the pension below it. Property tests in the repository check, for all inputs, that the plan meets both guarantees, that its rate is the smallest that does, and that before rounding its level never exceeds the triple lock's.

Two features follow from the rule. In its first year, April `{python} SWITCH`, the plan always pays what the triple lock pays: its earnings path starts from the `{python} fy(SWITCH - 1)` level, so the top-up is exactly the earnings rise whenever earnings lead. After that the plan pays less only after some earlier year in which the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR` ran ahead of earnings. Both rules pay that higher figure then, but it lifts the plan above its earnings path; when earnings next lead, the plan rises only by the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR` until earnings catch up, while the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level.

### If the plan had started earlier

```{python}
groups = D.history_groups()
unchanged = [g for g in groups if not g["changes"]]
check = D.EV["past_years_check"]
gap_final_ratio = 100 * (1 - past_weekly / actual_weekly)
mh = D.HISTORY["model_years"]
less_years = [y for y in D.HISTORY["years"]
              if round((first_group["bp_rate"][str(y)] - first_group["tl_rate"][str(y)]) * 1000) < 0]
spike = max(rec, key=lambda r: r["cpi"])
```

@fig-past applies the plan's rule to the published inputs from an earlier April. Started in `{python} first_group["label"]`, it would have paid `{python} wk(past_weekly)` a week in full new State Pension in `{python} fy(last_hist)`, against the `{python} wk(actual_weekly)` actually paid: `{python} pct(gap_final_ratio)` less. It pays less than the triple lock in April `{python} listing(less_years)`: each time the plan is still above its earnings path after earlier years in which CPI or the floor ran ahead of earnings. The largest shortfalls follow April `{python} spike["year"]`, when September CPI of `{python} rate(spike["cpi"])` set a rise far above earnings growth of `{python} rate(spike["earnings"])`. Started in `{python} listing([g["label"] for g in unchanged], "or")`, the plan would have paid the same as the triple lock every year to April `{python} D.HISTORY["years"][-1]`. The plan's earnings path here also grows by CPI in April `{python} susp_year`, as if the suspension of the earnings link applied to it too; with the published figure its earnings path would have been higher from then on, and the shortfalls here smaller.

For `{python} fy(mh[0])` to `{python} fy(mh[-1])`, the years the survey data cover, the savings are full model runs in which every flat-rate pension is set to the plan's level instead of the triple lock's. Had the plan started in `{python} first_group["label"]`, State Pension spending in `{python} fy(last_hist)` would have been `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"])` lower, and the government would have been `{python} bn(past_saving["net"])` better off once income tax and benefits respond.

The same comparison tests the monthly model behind our paths, before any shift. Fitted only on data to December `{python} check["years"][0] - 1`, and with no calibration because no forecast covers those years, the monthly model of @sec-step3 gives a plan started in April `{python} check["years"][0] + 1` an average gap of `{python} pct(check["model"]["mean_gap_pct"])` of the pension by April `{python} check["years"][1] + 1`. What happened gives `{python} pct(check["realised_gap_pct"])`, at the `{python} ordinal(check["model"]["realised_percentile"])` percentile of the model's paths. The same model tilted to match the dynamics of `{python} check["dynamics_targets"]["years"][0]`–`{python} check["dynamics_targets"]["years"][1]` averages `{python} pct(check["dynamics"]["mean_gap_pct"])` and puts what happened at its `{python} ordinal(check["dynamics"]["realised_percentile"])` percentile (@sec-calibration).

## The OBR's central forecast {#sec-step2}

```{python}
cp = D.CENTRAL["path"]
crows = D.path_rows(central)
a27 = cp["april_2027_inputs"]
floor_years = [r["year"] for r in crows if r["tl_source"] == "floor"]
after = [r for r in crows if r["year"] >= SWITCH]
floor_after = [r["year"] for r in after if r["tl_source"] in ("floor", "cpi")]
first_earn = next(r for r in after if r["tl_source"] == "earnings")
differ = [r for r in crows if D.differs(r)]
cal_src = cp["calendar_source"]
stat_src = cp["statutory_source"]
efo_years = [int(y) for y, s in cal_src.items() if s == "efo_calendar"]
lted_years = [int(y) for y, s in cal_src.items() if s == "lted_converted"]
q_years = [int(y) + 1 for y, s in stat_src.items() if s == "efo_quarterly"]
c_mid = D.row(central, MID)
c_flag = D.flagged_years(central)
SHORT_TL = {"earnings": "earnings", "cpi": "CPI", "floor": "floor"}
SHORT_BP = {"triple_lock": "triple lock", "earnings_path": "earnings path", "cpi": "CPI", "floor": "floor"}
```

### The central path and its sources

The central path uses the OBR's March 2026 Economic and fiscal outlook (EFO) for calendar-year CPI and average earnings growth in `{python} efo_years[0]`–`{python} efo_years[-1]` [@obr_efo2026], and its long-term economic determinants for `{python} lted_years[0]`–`{python} lted_years[-1]`, converted from fiscal to calendar years [@obr_lted2026]. After 2030 the OBR describes the determinants as a long-term projection, not a forecast. In the determinants calendar-year CPI settles at `{python} rate(cp["calendar"]["cpi"][str(FINAL)])` and earnings growth rises to `{python} rate(cp["calendar"]["earnings"][str(FINAL)])` by `{python} FINAL`.

The inputs to each April's rise are taken as close to the statutory timing as the forecasts allow (@tbl-central). April 2027's rise uses the published May–July 2026 earnings growth, `{python} rate(a27["earnings"])`, and August 2026 CPI, `{python} rate(a27["cpi"])`, standing in for September's, which ONS publishes on 21 October 2026. CPI would have to rise by more than `{python} points(a27["cpi_rise_needed_to_set_triple_lock"], 1)` points from August to September to overtake earnings growth; its largest August-to-September rise since `{python} a27["aug_to_sep_years"][0]` is `{python} points(a27["largest_aug_to_sep_cpi_rise"], 1)` points. The rises of April `{python} listing(q_years)` use the EFO's September-quarter CPI and April–June earnings growth, and later rises the calendar-year path, for which no quarterly forecast exists.

### The two rules on the central path

@fig-central shows both rules on this path. Earnings grow by less than `{python} FLOOR` for several years, so the floor sets the triple lock in April `{python} listing(floor_years)`. From April `{python} first_earn["year"]` earnings lead every year. The two rules differ in `{python} words(len(differ))` years: `{python} listing([f'April {r["year"]} (triple lock {rate(r["tl_rate"])}, set by {D.TL_SOURCE[r["tl_source"]]}; plan {rate(r["bp_rate"])}, {"rising to its earnings path" if r["bp_source"] == "earnings_path" else "set by the " + D.BP_SOURCE[r["bp_source"]]})' for r in differ])`. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} wk(c_final["tl_weekly"])` a week under the triple lock and `{python} wk(c_final["bp_weekly"])` under the plan, `{python} pct(D.gap_pct(c_final), 1)` lower.

### Why the saving is small on this path

The whole difference on the central path comes from the floor years just after the switch, April `{python} listing(floor_after)`. The plan pays the floor then too, but earnings grow by less, so the plan's pension ends up above its earnings path. When earnings pick up, the plan rises by only the floor, and then by what brings it back to its earnings path, while the triple lock rises with earnings from the higher level. Once the plan is back on its earnings path both rules rise with earnings, and the gap stays where the floor years left it. The plan saves `{python} bn(c_mid["gross"])` in State Pension spending in `{python} fy(MID)` and `{python} bn(c_final["gross"])` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`; net of income tax and benefits, `{python} bn(c_mid["net"])` and `{python} bn(c_final["net"])` (@tbl-central).

On a single path like this the triple lock rises with earnings in the long run: the ratchet pays out only when the lead passes between earnings and the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR`. The central path has no such reversals after `{python} first_earn["year"]`. The OBR's long-term projections instead assume a triple-lock premium of `{python} obr_premium` points a year over earnings [@obr_lted2026]; @sec-premium compares that with the premium across our paths.

In `{python} listing([fy(r["year"]) for r in c_flag])` the net saving on this path is `{python} listing([bn(r["net"]) for r in c_flag])`, far below the gross: one survey household's income rises by `{python} listing([bn(r["record_bn"]) for r in c_flag])` in total across the households it represents (@sec-record).

## Another path {#sec-step3}

```{python}
rrows = D.path_rows(rnd)
r_final = D.row(rnd, FINAL)
r_after = [r for r in rrows if r["year"] >= SWITCH]
reversals = sum(1 for a, b in zip(r_after, r_after[1:]) if a["tl_source"] != b["tl_source"])
r_differ = [r for r in rrows if D.differs(r)]
cpi_year = next(r["year"] for r in r_after if r["tl_source"] == "cpi")
m = D.EV["draws"]["model"]
drift = m["drift"]["annualised_pp_by_year"]
models = D.TRAJ["models"]
low = D.TRAJ["gap_statistics"]["lowest_september_cpi"]
deflation = min(models["tcop"]["september_cpi_below"], key=lambda k: float(k.rstrip("%")))
MONTHS = ["January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August", "September", "October",
          "November", "December"]
# Rises where the plan pays less than the triple lock while both follow earnings: the rounding case.
rounding = [r for r in r_differ if r["tl_source"] == "earnings" and r["bp_source"] == "earnings_path"
            and D.row(rnd, r["year"] - 1)["bp_source"] == "earnings_path"]
```

### A random path

The central forecast is one path of many. @fig-random runs both rules on a path drawn at random from the `{python} count(D.EV["draws"]["n"])` paths behind the expected saving of @sec-step6: `{python} lower1(rnd["source"])`, at the `{python} ordinal(rnd["selection"]["gap_percentile_2039"])` percentile of those paths: `{python} pct(rnd["selection"]["larger_gap_pct_2039"], 0)` of them open a bigger gap by then, so the saving on this one is small. We keep it because it was drawn at random; the middle and 90th-percentile paths below give the context.

On this path the figure that sets the triple lock changes `{python} {1: "once", 2: "twice"}.get(reversals, words(reversals) + " times")` from April `{python} SWITCH`, and the rules differ in `{python} words(len(r_differ))` years: `{python} listing([f'April {r["year"]} (triple lock {rate(r["tl_rate"])}, {D.TL_SOURCE[r["tl_source"]]}; plan {rate(r["bp_rate"])}, rising to its earnings path)' for r in r_differ])`. In April `{python} cpi_year` CPI runs ahead of earnings and both rules pay it; that lifts the plan above its earnings path, and the next year, when earnings lead, the plan rises only as far as its earnings path. `{python} (f"In April {rounding[0]['year']} the plan's rate is {TENTH} point below the triple lock's although both follow earnings: the year before, the plan's rise to its earnings path was rounded up, leaving it just above the path, so it needed slightly less than the earnings rise.") if rounding else ""` By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} wk(r_final["tl_weekly"])` a week under the triple lock and `{python} wk(r_final["bp_weekly"])` under the plan.

### How the monthly model makes the paths

The paths come from a model of the months themselves, since the triple lock's inputs are measured over different months from the calendar-year figures the OBR forecasts. It is a vector autoregression on the monthly log changes in the CPI index [@ons_d7bt] and in the whole-economy AWE total pay level [@ons_kab9], with an intercept and month dummies, fitted by least squares from 2000 to the latest published month. The lag order is chosen by the Bayesian information criterion (it picks `{python} words(m["lag_order"])`). The furlough months of 2020–21 are left out of the fit and of the pool of shocks, because their earnings changes reflect who was paid rather than what pay did. Each simulated month draws a pair of fitted residuals at random, so the shocks to prices and earnings keep their joint distribution; the one month for which CPI is published but AWE is not draws its earnings shock from its normal distribution given the observed CPI shock. From the simulated months come both the statutory inputs (September CPI, May–July earnings growth) and the calendar-year growth that the rest of the model uses, so the two stay consistent on every path. Calendar-year AWE total pay stands in for the OBR's measure of average earnings.

The model's own averages sit well away from the OBR's forecast, so every path is shifted by the same monthly drift: the smoothest drift that makes the paths' mean calendar-year CPI and earnings growth equal the central path in every year from `{python} D.YEARS[0]` to `{python} FINAL`. It starts in `{python} MONTHS[m["drift"]["first_month"][1] - 1]` `{python} m["drift"]["first_month"][0]`, the first month for which neither series is published. The drift is not small: it moves earnings growth by `{python} num(drift[str(D.YEARS[0])]["earnings"], 2)` points a year in `{python} D.YEARS[0]` and CPI growth by `{python} num(drift[str(FINAL)]["cpi"], 2)` points a year by `{python} FINAL`. Because every path moves by the same amount, each path's ups and downs, and the link between prices and earnings, remain the model's own. Tilting the weights of the paths to the same means instead [@robertson2005] leaves about `{python} count(D.EV["calibrations"]["means_tilt"]["ess"])` effective paths of `{python} count(D.EV["draws"]["n"])`; a drift held constant within each year would oscillate between years and put false reversals into the statutory inputs.

The same model with Student-t or Gaussian shocks is summarised in the results but not run in full: those shocks give years of falling prices more often, including September CPI below `{python} num(float(deflation.rstrip("%")), 0)`%, while the lowest September CPI since `{python} low["years"][0]` is `{python} rate(low["rate"])` (`{python} low["year"]`).

On the middle path the plan saves `{python} bn(D.row(p50, FINAL)["gross"])` in `{python} fy(FINAL)` (`{python} bn(D.row(p50, FINAL)["net"])` net), and on the 90th-percentile path `{python} bn(D.row(p90, FINAL)["gross"])` (`{python} bn(D.row(p90, FINAL)["net"])` net). @tbl-paths sets out all four paths.

## One pensioner {#sec-step4}

```{python}
exs = D.examples(rnd)
Y = FINAL
ex_rows = [(k, ex, D.borne_share(ex, Y)) for k, ex in exs.items()]
own, priv, soc, basic = (exs[k] for k in ("owner", "private_pension", "social_renter", "basic_renter"))
letter = {k: l for k, l in zip(exs, "abcd")}
sp_loss = -D.ex_change(own, "state_pension", Y)
tax_fall = -D.ex_change(own, "income_tax", Y)
pc_rise = D.ex_change(own, "pension_credit", Y)
ctr_rise = D.ex_change(own, "council_tax_reduction", Y)
# Years in which the owner bears part of the cut, and those in which it bears most of it.
own_part = [y for y in D.YEARS if D.ex_change(own, "net_income", y) < -0.5]
own_most = [y for y in own_part if D.ex_change(own, "net_income", y) < 0.5 * D.ex_change(own, "state_pension", y)]
# Where the Winter Fuel Payment changes, on any path shown.
wfp = []
for pid in D.PATH_IDS:
    for k, ex in D.examples(D.path(pid)).items():
        for y in D.YEARS:
            d = D.ex_change(ex, "winter_fuel_payment", y)
            if abs(d) > 0.005:
                wfp.append((pid, k, y, d))
assert not [w for w in wfp if w[0] == "random"]  # the text says it does not change on the random path
# The basic-pension example: years in which it bears part of the cut.
basic_part = [y for y in D.YEARS if D.ex_change(basic, "state_pension", y) < -0.5
              and D.ex_change(basic, "net_income", y) < -0.5]
def pc_share(ex, y):
    after_tax = -(D.ex_change(ex, "state_pension", y) - D.ex_change(ex, "income_tax", y))
    return D.ex_change(ex, "pension_credit", y) / after_tax
# The renters' Housing Benefit already covers the full rent when it does not change.
renter_hb_flat = all(abs(D.ex_change(e, "housing_benefit", y)) < 0.005 for e in (soc, basic) for y in D.YEARS)
p90_soc = D.examples(p90)["social_renter"]
PATH_WORDS = {"central": "central", "random": "random", "monthly_p50": "middle", "monthly_p90": "90th-percentile"}
def wfp_sentence():
    if not wfp:
        return "It does not change on the other paths either."
    parts = []
    for k, y in sorted({(w[1], w[2]) for w in wfp}):
        on = [PATH_WORDS[w[0]] for w in wfp if w[1] == k and w[2] == y]
        amount = max(w[3] for w in wfp if w[1] == k and w[2] == y)
        parts.append(f"for pensioner ({letter[k]}) in {fy(y)} on the {listing(on)} paths, where the plan's lower pension "
                     f"brings that pensioner's taxable income under the threshold and the payment of {gbp(amount)} "
                     f"offsets part of the loss")
    return "It changes " + listing(parts, sep="; ") + "."
mid_loss = p50["households_affected"][str(FINAL)]
```

The same random path runs four example pensioners through PolicyEngine UK as households, once under each rule (@fig-pensioners, @tbl-pensioners). Each receives the full flat-rate State Pension, claims everything it is entitled to, and is the stated age in every year: the examples describe a pensioner of that age in each year, not one person ageing. Their private pensions, rents and council tax are set in 2026-27 terms and grow with the path's CPI; the renters are existing Housing Benefit claimants, which policyengine-uk requires before it pays Housing Benefit. The examples are hypothetical households, not survey records. Because this path is near the bottom of the model's range, their losses are small; on the middle path the pension cut in `{python} fy(Y)` is `{python} gbp(-D.ex_change(D.examples(p50)["owner"], "state_pension", Y))` a year rather than `{python} gbp(sp_loss)`.

A lower State Pension means less income tax for a pensioner above the personal allowance, more Pension Credit for one entitled to it, more council tax reduction or Housing Benefit for one receiving them, and it can bring a pensioner back under the Winter Fuel Payment's income threshold. In `{python} fy(Y)` a pensioner on the new State Pension loses `{python} gbp(sp_loss, 2)` a year of pension under the plan on this path.

* **With a private pension** (pensioner (`{python} letter["private_pension"]`), `{python} lower1(priv["meta"]["label"])`), the pensioner pays `{python} gbp(-D.ex_change(priv, "income_tax", Y), 2)` less income tax and bears the rest: `{python} pct(100 * D.borne_share(priv, Y), 0)` of the loss.
* **With the State Pension only** (pensioner (`{python} letter["owner"]`), `{python} lower1(own["meta"]["label"])`), the pensioner's income after tax is below the Pension Credit guarantee in `{python} fy(Y)`, so Pension Credit rises by `{python} gbp(pc_rise, 2)`: exactly the fall in the pension after the `{python} gbp(tax_fall, 2)` fall in income tax. Pension Credit counts income after tax, both in the regulations [@spc2002, regulation 17(10)] and in policyengine-uk, so the two together replace the whole loss: in law the pensioner comes out even. The council renter on the same pension (pensioner (`{python} letter["social_renter"]`)) comes out the same way. In `{python} listing([fy(y) for y in own_part])` their income after tax is above the guarantee or only just below it, so both bear part of the cut, and most of it in `{python} listing([fy(y) for y in own_most])` (@fig-pensioners).
* **Council tax reduction** then adds about `{python} gbp(ctr_rise)` for both in `{python} fy(Y)`, so in the model they come out about `{python} gbp(D.ex_change(own, "net_income", Y))` a year ahead. That is a gap in the model, not in the plan. In England's pensioner scheme policyengine-uk tapers council tax reduction on income after tax without counting Pension Credit, so it rises by `{python} pct(100 * ctr_rise / pc_rise, 0)` of the after-tax loss that Pension Credit replaces; and it does not disregard the income of people receiving the guarantee credit, as the regulations require [@si2012_2885, Schedule 1, paragraph 13]. In law their council tax reduction would not change, and they would come out even.
* **On the old basic State Pension** (pensioner (`{python} letter["basic_renter"]`), `{python} lower1(basic["meta"]["label"])`), the pension loss is smaller, `{python} gbp(-D.ex_change(basic, "state_pension", Y), 2)`, and Pension Credit and income tax replace all of it in `{python} fy(Y)`. In `{python} listing([fy(y) for y in basic_part])` this pensioner does bear part of the cut: its Pension Credit then includes savings credit, which in policyengine-uk phases in with income above a threshold, so a lower pension also lowers the savings credit, and Pension Credit rises by only `{python} pct(100 * pc_share(basic, basic_part[0]), 0)` of the after-tax loss.

`{python} "The renters' Housing Benefit does not change in any year on this path: it already covers the full rent, so it cannot rise." if renter_hb_flat else ""`

```{python}
    if s <= 0:

    return pct(100 * s, 0)
body.append(["Share of the pension loss borne", *[borne(ex, s) for _, ex, s in ex_rows]])
display(Markdown(md_table(heads, body, "lrrrr") + "\n\nThe examples: " +
                 "; ".join(f"({l}) {lower1(ex['meta']['label'])}" for l, (_, ex, _) in zip("abcd", ex_rows)) + "."))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-pensioners
```

The Winter Fuel Payment does not change for any example on the random path. In policyengine-uk it is paid, outside Scotland, to pensioners on Pension Credit or certain other income-related benefits and, in England and Wales, to households in which a pensioner's taxable income is below a fixed threshold. `{python} wfp_sentence()`

On the 90th-percentile path the council renter shows a larger step. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` its State Pension is `{python} gbp(-D.ex_change(p90_soc, "state_pension", FINAL))` lower under the plan, which brings it onto the Pension Credit guarantee credit. In policyengine-uk a pensioner receiving the guarantee credit has no income counted in the Housing Benefit means test, so its Housing Benefit rises by `{python} gbp(D.ex_change(p90_soc, "housing_benefit", FINAL))` to the maximum and its income by `{python} gbp(D.ex_change(p90_soc, "net_income", FINAL))`. The step is this large partly because of how the runs uprate: they raise the Pension Credit guarantee with earnings, as the law requires at least, while policyengine-uk raises the Housing Benefit personal allowance for pensioners with CPI. The allowance starts above the guarantee, but on paths where earnings outgrow prices the guarantee overtakes it, and from then on a pensioner moving onto guarantee credit moves from a tapered Housing Benefit award to the maximum in one step. A step of this kind is the likely source of the single-household effects in @sec-record.

The same random path runs through PolicyEngine UK for the whole survey population, once under each rule. Every pensioner's State Pension is recalculated, and with it their income tax, Pension Credit, Housing Benefit, council tax reduction and Winter Fuel Payment. The gross saving is the fall in spending on the basic and new State Pension; the net saving is the change in the government's balance once taxes and benefits respond. ### Gross and net saving by year

On the random path the plan first saves money in `{python} fy(first_saving["year"])`, `{python} bn(first_saving["gross"])` gross, and by `{python} fy(FINAL)` it saves `{python} bn(r_final["gross"])` gross and `{python} bn(r_final["net"])` net (@fig-savings, @tbl-random).

### From gross to net

@tbl-account follows the gross saving to the net saving. In `{python} fy(FINAL)` extra Pension Credit takes `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][0][1])` of the `{python} bn(acc["gross"])` gross saving back, lower income tax `{python} bn(-acc["rows"][5][1])` and the other offsets `{python} bn(acc["gross"] - acc["net"] + acc["rows"][0][1] + acc["rows"][5][1])`, leaving `{python} bn(acc["net"])`: `{python} pct(100 * acc["net"] / acc["gross"], 0)` of the gross.

Several features of the runs move the offsets, in both directions. Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them, so nobody the plan makes newly entitled starts claiming, which makes their offsets smaller and the net saving larger. In policyengine-uk, Housing Benefit goes only to a benefit unit that reports receiving it. Council tax reduction goes to one that reports receiving it, or to any benefit unit if none in the whole simulation reports any of several other means-tested benefits; since some benefit units in the Enhanced FRS report one, that second test fails for every benefit unit. Rents and council tax stay at their 2030 amounts after 2030, which lowers the most either benefit can pay and probably shrinks both offsets too. The Enhanced FRS puts Pension Credit claims and pension-age Housing Benefit above DWP's figures (@tbl-coverage), which makes those offsets larger and the net saving smaller.

```{python}
body.append(["Everything else (other taxes and benefits)", num(acc_mid["other"], 3), num(acc["other"], 3)])
body.append(["**Saving to the government (net)**", f'**{num(acc_mid["net"], 3)}**', f'**{num(acc["net"], 3)}**'])
display(Markdown(md_table(["", fy(MID), fy(FINAL)], body)))
```

### Who loses

In `{python} fy(FINAL)`, `{python} pct(aff["losing_pct"])` of households have a lower income under the plan on this path (by more than £1 a year), losing `{python} gbp(aff["mean_loss_gbp"])` a year on average; on the middle path the share is similar, `{python} pct(mid_loss["losing_pct"])`, but the mean loss is `{python} gbp(mid_loss["mean_loss_gbp"])`. By income quintile (@tbl-quintiles) the mean loss is largest in the `{python} listing([ordinal(q["quintile"]) for q in sorted(quint, key=lambda q: q["mean_change_gbp"])[:2]])` quintiles and smallest in the `{python} ordinal(max(quint, key=lambda q: q["mean_change_gbp"])["quintile"])`; relative to income the `{python} ordinal(min(quint, key=lambda q: q["pct_income_change"])["quintile"])` quintile loses most, `{python} pct(abs(min(q["pct_income_change"] for q in quint)), 3)` of its income.

### One survey household {#sec-record}

```{python}
rf = r_flag
ev_rec = D.est("net_excluding_largest_record", FINAL)
ev_rec_mid = D.est("net_excluding_largest_record", MID)
same = len({num(r["record_bn"], 2) for r in rf}) == 1
typical = [r for r in rrows if r["year"] >= SWITCH and abs(r["record_share"]) < D.RECORD_FLAG and r["gross"] > 0]
```

A pension cut of a few pounds a week can move one survey household across a threshold, such as the step onto guarantee credit and the maximum Housing Benefit described above, and if that household carries a large survey weight the step moves the national figure. Every run records, for every year, the single household record whose income changes most in total, as its contribution to the change in households' income (£ billion) and its share of that change. The FRS is licensed data, so the results give nothing else about the record.

On the random path one record carries a fifth or more of the change in `{python} listing([fy(r["year"]) for r in rf])`: it gains `{python} (bn(rf[0]["record_bn"]) + " in each year") if same else listing([bn(r["record_bn"]) for r in rf])` while households as a whole lose, so it carries `{python} listing([pct(100 * abs(r["record_share"]), 0) for r in rf])` of the total change, with the opposite sign. Without it the net saving in those years would be `{python} listing([bn(r["net"] + r["record_bn"]) for r in rf])` instead of `{python} listing([bn(r["net"]) for r in rf])` (@tbl-random). In the other years after the first saving the largest record carries about `{python} pct(100 * abs(typical[-1]["record_share"]), 0)` of the change. The gross saving has no such thresholds: it comes only from the flat rates. Across all the paths of @sec-step6, removing each path's largest record changes the expected net saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` only from `{python} bn(n_final["mean"])` to `{python} bn(ev_rec["mean"])`, and in `{python} fy(MID)` from `{python} bn(D.est("net", MID)["mean"])` to `{python} bn(ev_rec_mid["mean"])`.

```{python}
                           "Largest record, £ billion", "Its share"], body)))
```

## Every path {#sec-step6}

```{python}
strata = D.EV["strata"]
ident = D.EV["identical_rates"]
yrs_show = [y for y in D.YEARS if y >= SWITCH]
est_mid = D.est("gross", MID)
comp = {k: D.est(f"component.{k}", FINAL) for k in ("pension_credit", "housing_benefit", "income_tax")}
runs_f = [(p["gap_2039_gbp_week"], p["outputs"]["primary"]["gross"][str(FINAL)]) for p in D.EV["paths"]
          if p["gap_2039_gbp_week"] > 1]
ratios = [g / x for x, g in runs_f]
slope = sum(ratios) / len(ratios)
assert max(ratios) / min(ratios) - 1 < 1e-4  # the text says the ratio is the same in every run
rec_fin = [p["outputs"]["primary"]["largest_record_bn"][str(FINAL)] for p in D.EV["paths"]]
se_before = D.est("gross", FINAL - 1)["se"]
```

### The expected saving

A single path cannot give the saving to expect, because the saving comes from years in which CPI or the floor runs ahead of earnings, and the central path has almost none after the switch: the saving on the average path is not the average saving. We therefore average the saving over the model's paths of @sec-step3, estimated from full runs of both rules on `{python} count(D.n_unique())` of them. @fig-expected and @tbl-expected give the expected saving by year with its Monte Carlo standard error, which measures how precisely those runs pin down the average over all `{python} count(D.EV["draws"]["n"])` paths. It is not the range of outcomes, and it does not cover the choice of model or calibration (@sec-calibration).

In `{python} fy(FINAL)` the expected saving is `{python} pm(g_final)` gross and `{python} pm(n_final)` net. Of the gross saving, extra Pension Credit takes back `{python} bn(comp["pension_credit"]["mean"])`, lower income tax `{python} bn(-comp["income_tax"]["mean"])` and extra Housing Benefit `{python} bn(comp["housing_benefit"]["mean"])`. In `{python} fy(MID)`, `{python} words(MID - SWITCH + 1)` rises after the switch, the expected gross saving is `{python} pm(est_mid)`. The central path alone gives `{python} bn(c_final["gross"])` in `{python} fy(FINAL)`. The standard error is smallest in `{python} fy(FINAL)` (`{python} bn(g_final["se"], 3)`, against `{python} bn(se_before, 3)` a year earlier) because the paths are stratified on that year's gap, which fixes the gross saving closely within each stratum.

The saving on any one path can be far from the expected saving, which the standard error does not measure. By `{python} fy(FINAL)` the full new State Pension is `{python} wk(gap["mean_gap_gbp_week"])` a week lower under the plan on average across the paths, but the gap runs from `{python} wk(gap["gap_gbp_week"]["p10"])` at the 10th percentile of paths to `{python} wk(gap["gap_gbp_week"]["p90"])` at the 90th (rule arithmetic). That spread describes the model's scenarios; @sec-appendix-backtest explains why we do not read it as a forecast probability. @fig-runs shows each full run's `{python} fy(FINAL)` saving against its weekly gap. The gross saving is `{python} bn(slope, 3)` for each £1 a week of gap in every run: it comes only from the flat rates. The net saving scatters around a lower line, and the runs furthest below it are those in which one survey household gains, by up to `{python} bn(max(rec_fin))` (@sec-record).

```{python}
#| label: fig-expected
#| fig-cap: "The expected saving from the Burnham plan by fiscal year, gross (State Pension spending) and net (the government's balance), with ±1.96 Monte Carlo standard errors (shaded: the precision of the average, not the range of outcomes), and the gross saving on the central forecast alone. Weighted means of full model runs on the Enhanced FRS."
F.expected();
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-expected
#| tbl-cap: "The expected saving by fiscal year, £ billion, with Monte Carlo standard errors (SE), the expected share of households losing more than £1 a year, and the gross saving on the central path alone."
body = []
for y in yrs_show:
    g, n, l = D.est("gross", y), D.est("net", y), D.est("households_losing_pct", y)
    body.append([fy(y), num(g["mean"], 2), num(g["se"], 2), num(n["mean"], 2), num(n["se"], 2),
                 pct(l["mean"]), num(D.row(central, y)["gross"], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Year", "Gross", "SE", "Net", "SE", "Households losing", "Central path, gross"], body)))
```

```{python}

#| fig-cap: "Every full run behind the expected saving: the saving in the final year against the gap in the full new State Pension on that path. One point per run; the runs carry different weights in the estimate (by stratum)."
```

### Strata and estimator

```{python}
W_ident = ident["probability"]
top = strata[-1]
```

The `{python} count(D.EV["draws"]["n"])` paths are not all run. Paths on which the two rules pay the same rise every year save exactly nothing, since both runs get identical inputs; they are `{python} pct(100 * W_ident, 2)` of paths, form their own stratum, and one is run to confirm it (its largest saving in any year is `{python} bn(ident["check_run"]["largest_abs_saving_bn"])`). The rest are split into `{python} words(len(strata))` strata, each holding an equal share of the paths, by the gap in the full new State Pension in `{python} fy(FINAL)`, which the rule arithmetic gives for every path before any model run. `{python} count(D.n_runs())` draws are allocated across the strata in proportion to each stratum's share of paths times the spread of the gap within it [@neyman1934], with at least two a stratum, and drawn at random with replacement within each stratum (every path has the same weight under the primary calibration). They are `{python} count(D.n_unique())` distinct paths, each a full run. The top stratum, with the widest spread, gets `{python} top["paths"]` draws (@tbl-strata).

For any output $y$ the estimate is $\hat{\mu} = \sum_h W_h \bar{y}_h$, where $W_h$ is stratum $h$'s share of the paths and $\bar{y}_h$ the mean over its draws, and its Monte Carlo standard error is $\sqrt{\sum_h W_h^2 s_h^2 / n_h}$, with $s_h$ the standard deviation and $n_h$ the number of draws in the stratum. The stratum of identical rules adds exactly zero. Tests in the repository check that the estimator is unbiased and that its interval covers about 95% of the time on synthetic cases, and that the published estimates recompute from the per-path records in the results file.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-strata
#| tbl-cap: "The strata: each an equal share of the paths on which the rules differ, by the final-year weekly gap (rule arithmetic), and the draws in each (a path drawn twice is run once)."
body = [[s["stratum"], pct(100 * s["probability"], 2), f'{wk(s["gap_range_gbp_week"][0])} to {wk(s["gap_range_gbp_week"][1])}',
         s["paths"], s["unique_paths"], s["sensitivity_paths"]] for s in strata]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Stratum", "Share of paths", f"Gap in {fy(FINAL)}, £ a week", "Draws", "Distinct paths",
                           "Also on Microcosm"], body, "rrrrrr")))
```

### Choosing the calibration {#sec-calibration}

```{python}
bt = D.EV["backtest"]
law = bt["summary"]["suspended"]
pub = bt["summary"]["published"]
def bias(r):
    return f'{"+" if r["bias_pct_points"] >= 0 else "−"}{num(abs(r["bias_pct_points"]), 2)} ± {num(r["bias_se_independent"], 2)}'
lower_mae = law["shift_dynamics"]["mean_abs_error"] < law["means_shift"]["mean_abs_error"]
larger_both = (abs(law["shift_dynamics"]["bias_pct_points"]) > abs(law["means_shift"]["bias_pct_points"])
               and abs(pub["shift_dynamics"]["bias_pct_points"]) > abs(pub["means_shift"]["bias_pct_points"]))
worst_obr = all(max(s, key=lambda k: abs(s[k]["bias_pct_points"])) == "obr_point" for s in (law, pub))
widest = max(sens, key=lambda k: sens[k]["gross"][str(FINAL)]["se"])
assert widest == min(sens, key=lambda k: sens[k]["effective_runs"])  # the text says the widest row rests on the fewest
```

The paths could be calibrated in more than one way. Besides matching the OBR's means, they could also be tilted, by entropy tilting [@robertson2005], so that the variance of the gap between May–July earnings and September CPI, and how often the lead passes between them, match history. We chose between these on two tests of the expected gap between the two rules, not of the saving, since the gap is what the calibration changes.

The first is a chronological backtest over `{python} words(len(bt["origins"]))` OBR forecasts in the OBR's historical official forecasts database [@obr_hofd2026], from the `{python} bt["origins"][0]` to the `{python} bt["origins"][-1]`. At each, the monthly model is fitted only on data to the December before the forecast, and the calibrations take the forecast's calendar-year CPI and earnings as the means; the plan starts at the April rise two years after the forecast, and the gap is measured after `{python} words(H)` rises. @tbl-backtest compares each method's expected gap with what happened, scoring April 2022 both as in law (earnings suspended) and with the published earnings. Of the calibrations that match the OBR's means, which the expected value needs, the drift shift and entropy tilting to the means have almost the same bias: `{python} bias(law["means_shift"])` and `{python} bias(law["means_tilt"])` points of the pension as in law, each within one standard error of zero, and `{python} bias(pub["means_shift"])` and `{python} bias(pub["means_tilt"])` as published, about one standard error. We use the shift because tilting keeps so few effective paths. Tilting further, to past dynamics, made the bias `{python} "larger under both treatments" if larger_both else "different"` (`{python} bias(law["shift_dynamics"])` and `{python} bias(pub["shift_dynamics"])`)`{python} ", though its mean absolute error as in law is lower" if lower_mae else ""`; we chose on bias because the expected value is a mean. The uncalibrated model has the smallest bias as in law (`{python} bias(law["model"])`) but does not match the OBR's forecast. `{python} ("The OBR forecast used as a single path has the largest bias under both (" + bias(law["obr_point"]) + " and " + bias(pub["obr_point"]) + "): it expects too few changes of lead.") if worst_obr else ""` The origins overlap, sharing `{python} words(H - 1)` of `{python} words(H)` target years with their neighbours, so the standard errors, computed as if they were independent, understate the uncertainty; the data are today's revised figures, and the model design was chosen with the whole sample in view.

The second, the past-years check of @sec-step1, cannot test the drift shift, since no forecast covers those years; it bears only on tilting to past dynamics, which put what happened at the `{python} ordinal(check["dynamics"]["realised_percentile"])` percentile of its paths, against the `{python} ordinal(check["model"]["realised_percentile"])` for the model alone.

The tilts are kept as sensitivities, computed by reweighting the same full runs (@tbl-sensitivities). Across the `{python} words(len(sens))` of them the expected gross saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` runs from `{python} bn(min(sens_g))` to `{python} bn(max(sens_g))`, against `{python} bn(g_final["mean"])` for the primary calibration. Reweighting leaves few effective runs in some cases (as few as `{python} num(min(v["effective_runs"] for v in sens.values()), 0)` of `{python} count(D.n_runs())` draws), so those rows' standard errors are approximate and too narrow; the widest row rests on the fewest.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-backtest
#| tbl-cap: "The expected-value backtest: mean expected gap between the triple lock and the Burnham plan after the rises, % of the pension, and its bias (± standard error, treating the origins as independent) against what happened, with April 2022 as in law and as published."
body = []
for k, label in D.BACKTEST_LABELS.items():
    body.append([label, num(pub[k]["mean_predicted_gap_pct"], 2), bias(law[k]), bias(pub[k]),
                 num(law[k]["mean_abs_error"], 2), num(law[k]["switch_bias"], 2)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Method", "Expected gap", "Bias, in law", "Bias, published", "Mean absolute error, in law",
                           "Lead changes, predicted minus actual, in law"], body) +
                 f'\n\nRealised gap, averaged over the forecasts: {num(law["means_shift"]["mean_realised_gap_pct"], 2)}% as in law, '
                 f'{num(pub["means_shift"]["mean_realised_gap_pct"], 2)}% with April 2022 as published.'))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-sensitivities
#| tbl-cap: "The expected saving in the final year under other calibrations, £ billion (± 1.96 SE), from the same full runs reweighted. Each row keeps the OBR's means and tilts the shifted paths to a history window's gap variance and rate of lead changes (and, where shown, its share of years below the floor), with the furlough years and April 2022 treated as the Treatment column says. Effective runs measure how many of the draws the reweighting leaves in use."
body = [["Primary: drift shift only", "", "", f'{num(g_final["mean"], 2)} ± {num(1.96 * g_final["se"], 2)}',
         f'{num(n_final["mean"], 2)} ± {num(1.96 * n_final["se"], 2)}', count(D.EV["draws"]["n"]), count(D.n_runs())]]
for k, v in sens.items():
    g, n = v["gross"][str(FINAL)], v["net"][str(FINAL)]
    window, treatment, what = D.calibration_parts(k)
    body.append([window, treatment, what, f'{num(g["mean"], 2)} ± {num(1.96 * g["se"], 2)}',
                 f'{num(n["mean"], 2)} ± {num(1.96 * n["se"], 2)}', count(v["ess"]), num(v["effective_runs"], 0)])
display(Markdown(md_table(["History", "Treatment", "Tilted to", "Gross", "Net", "Effective paths", "Effective runs"],
                          body, "lllrrrr")))
```

### The Enhanced FRS and Microcosm

```{python}
pdiff = D.EV["paired_difference"]
g_s, n_s = D.est("gross", FINAL, "sensitivity"), D.est("net", FINAL, "sensitivity")
efrs_sub_g = g_s["mean"] - pdiff["gross"][str(FINAL)]["mean"]
efrs_sub_n = n_s["mean"] - pdiff["net"][str(FINAL)]["mean"]
cov = D.R["coverage"]
cov_rows = {r["key"]: r for r in cov["rows"]}
lose_s = D.est("households_losing_pct", FINAL, "sensitivity")
assert pdiff["gross"][str(FINAL)]["se"] < 0.005  # the text says "under £0.01bn"
```

The first `{python} D.n_sensitivity()` of the draws, spread across the strata, were also run on Microcosm, so the difference between the datasets is estimated from paired runs; with few runs in some strata, its standard errors are approximate. On those paths the expected gross saving in `{python} fy(FINAL)` is `{python} bn(efrs_sub_g)` on the Enhanced FRS and `{python} bn(g_s["mean"])` on Microcosm, `{python} bn(pdiff["gross"][str(FINAL)]["mean"])` higher (standard error under £0.01bn); the net saving is `{python} bn(efrs_sub_n)` and `{python} bn(n_s["mean"])`, `{python} bn(pdiff["net"][str(FINAL)]["mean"])` higher (standard error `{python} bn(pdiff["net"][str(FINAL)]["se"])`). On Microcosm `{python} pct(lose_s["mean"])` of households lose, against `{python} pct(lose_final["mean"])` on the Enhanced FRS (on all draws).

The gross saving scales with State Pension spending in the data: every run checks that each flat-rate pension moves exactly in proportion to the flat rate. @tbl-coverage sets both datasets against DWP's forecast for `{python} fy(cov["year"])` [@dwp_bect2026]. The Enhanced FRS puts basic and new State Pension spending at `{python} bn(cov_rows["flat_rate_bn"]["primary"], 1)`, against DWP's `{python} bn(cov_rows["flat_rate_bn"]["dwp"], 1)` (which includes payments abroad), and pension-age Housing Benefit at `{python} bn(cov_rows["housing_benefit_pension_age_bn"]["primary"], 1)`, against DWP's `{python} bn(cov_rows["housing_benefit_pension_age_bn"]["dwp"], 1)`. The first gap makes the gross saving smaller; the second, with Pension Credit claims above DWP's, can make the offsets larger.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-coverage
#| tbl-cap: "The survey data against DWP's Spring Forecast 2026 for 2026-27. DWP's tables cover Great Britain (plus benefits paid abroad where the tables do not separate them); the model covers the UK."
body = []
for r in cov["rows"]:
    f = (lambda v: f"{num(v, 2)}m") if r["key"].endswith("_m") else (lambda v: bn(v, 1))
    body.append([r["label"], f(r["dwp"]), f(r["primary"]), f(r["sensitivity"])])
display(Markdown(md_table(["2026-27", "DWP forecast", "Enhanced FRS", "Microcosm"], body)))
```

### DWP's costing

```{python}
dwp_caveat = re.search(r"These savings should not be used[^.]*", DWP_TEXT).group(0)
g90 = D.row(p90, FINAL)["gross"]
```

DWP costs the plan at £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn in `{python} fy(FINAL)` in cash terms (£`{python} dwp_real`bn in 2025-26 prices) [@dwp_uprating2026]. Our expected gross saving that year is `{python} bn(g_final["mean"])`. The figures differ for several reasons:

* DWP applies one uprating path, which it does not state; ours is an average over paths calibrated to the OBR's forecast. On the central path alone we find `{python} bn(c_final["gross"])`. For a single path to save £`{python} dwp_nominal`bn it needs several years in which CPI or the floor beats earnings; our 90th-percentile path saves `{python} bn(g90)` gross.
* DWP's model, `{python} D.DWP["model"].split(",")[0]`, projects the population and each person's pension. Our survey is not aged: ages stay at their survey values, top-coded at `{python} MAX_AGE`; each pensioner keeps the pension type they had in the survey, so no new pensioners join on the new State Pension; and the number of pensioners changes only through the survey weights and the rise in State Pension age to `{python} num(central["fixed_inputs"]["state_pension_age"][str(FINAL)][0], 0)`.
* The Enhanced FRS has less State Pension spending than DWP's forecast (@tbl-coverage).
* DWP's figure is direct spending for Great Britain, with no tax effects, `{python} re.search(r"rounded to the nearest [^;]+", D.DWP["coverage"]).group(0)`: it compares with our gross figure, for the UK.
* DWP cautions that "`{python} dwp_caveat`" [@dwp_uprating2026].

### The OBR's long-term premium {#sec-premium}

```{python}
gbc = D.EV["gap_by_calibration"]
tl_prem = [v["mean_rate_minus_earnings_2034_2039"]["triple_lock"] for k, v in gbc.items() if k != "model"]
```

The OBR's long-term projections assume the triple lock raises the pension `{python} obr_premium` percentage points a year faster than earnings [@obr_lted2026]. On our paths the triple lock rises `{python} points(prem["triple_lock"])` points a year faster than May–July earnings on average over the April rises of `{python} MID` to `{python} FINAL`; the Burnham plan rises `{python} points(abs(prem["burnham_2030"]))` points a year `{python} "slower" if prem["burnham_2030"] < 0 else "faster"`. Across the calibrations that match the OBR's means the triple lock's premium runs from `{python} points(min(tl_prem))` to `{python} points(max(tl_prem))` points. This is rule arithmetic on the inputs, not a fiscal figure, and it compares the triple lock's rise with the statutory earnings measure, where the OBR's premium is over its own measure of average earnings.

### Other published costings

```{python}
bmk = {b["id"]: b for b in D.R["benchmarks"]}
rf = bmk["rf_ratchet_2026_cumulative"]
rf_nums = re.findall(r"£(\d+(?:\.\d+)?)(?:bn| billion)", rf["figure_text"])
assert len(rf_nums) == 2, rf_nums  # the OBR's gross figure, then RF's net one
```

@tbl-benchmarks sets our closest figures beside other published costings. Only DWP's costing is of this plan; the others compare the triple lock with earnings uprating, over the years since 2012 or over a long horizon, so they are context, not checks. The OBR estimated in July 2025 that the triple lock would cost `{python} re.search(r"£[\d.]+ billion", bmk["obr_frs_2025"]["figure_text"]).group(0)` a year by 2029-30 against earnings uprating since 2012 [@obr_frs2025]. The Resolution Foundation cites the OBR's estimate that State Pension spending would be £`{python} rf_nums[0]`bn lower this year with earnings-linked uprating than with the triple lock, and puts the net saving at about £`{python} rf_nums[1]`bn after income tax and means-tested benefits [@rf_ratchet2026]. Had the Burnham plan, which keeps a floor of the higher of CPI and `{python} FLOOR`, started in `{python} first_group["label"]`, we find it would save `{python} bn(past_saving["gross"])` gross and `{python} bn(past_saving["net"])` net in `{python} fy(last_hist)`. The OBR's July 2026 report looks further ahead: state pension spending is "`{python} frs26_rise`", driven by ageing and triple-lock uprating, and with earnings uprating instead it "`{python} frs26_earn`" [@obr_frs2026]. The closest methodological precedent is the Institute for Fiscal Studies' simulation of the triple lock's cost from historical inflation and earnings [@cribb2023].

```{python}
#| label: tbl-benchmarks
#| tbl-cap: "Other published figures and our closest figure. 'Like for like' says whether the two measure the same thing."
LIKE = {"yes": "Yes", "partial": "Partly", "no": "No"}
def ours(b):
    v = b["our_value"]
    return f"{points(v)} points a year" if "rate_minus_earnings" in b["our_metric"] else bn(v, 2)
def theirs(b):
    if b["id"] == "rf_ratchet_2026_cumulative":
        return (f"State Pension spending £{rf_nums[0]}bn lower this year with earnings-linked uprating (the OBR's "
                f"estimate); about £{rf_nums[1]}bn net")
    t = b["figure_text"]
    if b["id"] == "dwp_uprating_2026":
        s = D.DWP["saving_bn"][str(FINAL)]
        return f"Savings against the triple lock of £{s['nominal']}bn in {fy(FINAL)} in cash terms, £{s['real_2025_26_prices']}bn in 2025-26 prices"
    if b["id"] == "obr_lted_triple_lock_premium":
        return "The 'Triple lock' growth rate: “" + re.search(r"Average earnings growth plus [^(]*points", t).group(0) + "”"
    if b["id"] == "obr_frs_2025":
        added = re.search(r"will have added .*? by \d{4}-\d{2}", t).group(0)
        initial = re.search(r"the £[\d.]+ billion we estimate .*? under initial assumptions", t).group(0)
        return f"“…{added}”, against “{initial}”"
    if b["id"] == "obr_frs_2026":
        return f"State pension spending “{frs26_rise}”; with earnings uprating it “{frs26_earn}”"
    return t
body = [[f'{b["publisher"]}, *{b["title"]}* ({b["date"]})', theirs(b), ours(b), LIKE[b["like_for_like"]]]
        for b in D.R["benchmarks"]]
display(Markdown(md_table(["Source", "Their figure", "Our closest figure", "Like for like"], body, "lllr") +
                 "\n\nAME: Annually Managed Expenditure."))
```

## Method and limitations {#sec-method}

### A path through PolicyEngine UK

A path is calendar-year CPI and earnings growth for `{python} D.YEARS[0]`–`{python} FINAL`, plus the statutory inputs that set the April rises. The calendar growth replaces the model's OBR growth assumptions for CPI and average earnings, with RPI and CPIH moved by the same amount as CPI, in a scenario applied before the data load: the model builds its derived series (uprating indices, the lagged CPI that uprates benefits, its own triple lock) when it loads parameters, so the same changes passed as a reform after loading would do nothing. The analysis first extends those derived series to 2042; without that, policyengine-uk's benefit rates stop following the path after April 2029.

Each run checks, in every year, that the model follows the path, and fails if any check misses: benefit rates uprated by CPI follow the path's calendar-year CPI of the year before (not September CPI, which uprates them in law); CPI-indexed thresholds follow it in the same year; employment income follows the path's earnings; the model's own triple lock and new State Pension follow the path; every flat-rate pension scales exactly by the ratio of the two rules' amounts; the model's adjustment of pay for changes in employer National Insurance is zero (a PolicyEngine scenario builds a second simulation on the model's default path as its baseline, and each run drops it so that nothing is compared with a different path); and the Pension Credit guarantee follows the path's earnings. Private pension income also moves, with the previous year's RPI up to a cap. Dividend, property, savings and self-employment income, rents and council tax do not follow the path, and each run records their growth. April 2027's benefit uprating is the model's own forecast of calendar-2026 CPI on every path, not September 2026 CPI.

### Inputs held the same under both rules

```{python}
fi = central["fixed_inputs"]
spa_final = fi["state_pension_age"][str(FINAL)][0]
spa_from = min(int(y) for y, v in fi["state_pension_age"].items() if v[0] == spa_final)
spa_before = fi["state_pension_age"][str(D.YEARS[0])][0]
```

Four inputs are set the same way under both rules, so that only the basic and new State Pension differ between the two runs of a path:

* **Pension type.** Each person's State Pension type (basic or new) is held at its survey-year value. Survey ages do not advance, and policyengine-uk decides the type from age each year, so it would otherwise move a cohort a year from the basic to the new State Pension while still paying its additional pension on the basic basis.
* **Additional State Pension.** The survey-year amount, grown by September CPI (published to April 2026, then the path's), for people over State Pension age that year.
* **State Pension age.** `{python} num(spa_final, 0)` from `{python} fy(spa_from)` [@pa2014]; the installed parameters stop at `{python} num(spa_before, 0)`. The Pensions Act 2014 phases the rise in by month of birth over 2026–28; with whole-year survey ages held fixed, the runs make it a single step, and the survey's `{python} num(spa_before, 0)`-year-olds are below State Pension age from then on.
* **Pension Credit guarantee.** The standard minimum guarantee rises with May–July earnings and is never cut, the minimum the law requires [@ssaa1992_s150a]; policyengine-uk uprates it by CPI. This is an assumption, the same under both rules.

### Jobs and reproducibility

Each model run is a job in its own process, cached under a hash of its arguments, the analysis code and the package versions, so an interrupted build resumes and any change to the engine reruns every job. The results in this paper were built at revision `{python} D.PROV["git_revision"][:7]` of PolicyEngine/uk-triple-lock with policyengine `{python} D.BUNDLE["policyengine_version"]`, policyengine-uk `{python} D.BUNDLE["model_version"]` and the Enhanced FRS `{python} D.BUNDLE["certified_data_build_id"]`. The manuscript reads `data/results.json` and computes every number it prints from it; the repository's README gives the commands to rebuild the file.

```{python}
def tidy(text):
    """The results file's limitation text, with en dashes in ranges."""
    text = text.replace("May-July", "May–July").replace("April-June", "April–June")
    return re.sub(r"\b(\d{4})-(\d{4})\b", r"\1–\2", text)


REPLACE = {
    # The file overstates single records' cause, and it says DWP "defines" what is our reading of DWP's description.
    # Its take-up limitation stands as written: in the survey runs policyengine-uk's claims_all_entitled_benefits,
    # which sums reported benefits over the whole simulation, is false for every benefit unit.
    "One such record moves some paths' net figures by billions of pounds;":
    "Single records move some paths' net figures by billions of pounds, most likely through this step;",
    "as DWP defines it;": "our reading of DWP's description;",
}
items = []
for l in D.R["method_limitations"]:
    for a, b in REPLACE.items():
        l = l.replace(a, b)
    items.append(tidy(l))
assert not any("as DWP defines it" in l for l in items)
assert any("Housing Benefit and council tax reduction respond only for households already receiving them" in l
           for l in items)
items.append(
    "The runs raise the Pension Credit guarantee with earnings while policyengine-uk raises the Housing Benefit "
    "personal allowance for pensioners with CPI. On paths where earnings outgrow prices the guarantee overtakes the "
    "allowance, and a pensioner moving onto guarantee credit then gains the maximum Housing Benefit in one step.")
display(Markdown("\n".join(f"* {l}" for l in items)))
```

## Appendix: which forecast distribution scores best {#sec-appendix-backtest .appendix}

```{python}
st = D.TRAJ["backtest"]["statutory"]
tr = st["treatments"]
def block(t):
    return tr[t]["chronological"]
origins = block("published")["origins"]
def ranges(t):
    return {k: v for k, v in block(t)["methods"].items() if k != "obr_point"}
def best(t):
    rs = ranges(t)
    b = max(v["burnham_2030_inside"] for v in rs.values())
    leader = min((k for k, v in rs.items() if v["burnham_2030_inside"] == b), key=lambda k: rs[k]["burnham_2030_crps_pp"])
    missed = [o for o, hit in zip(origins, rs[leader]["burnham_2030_inside_by_origin"]) if not hit]
    return b, leader, missed
b_pub, lead_pub, _ = best("published")
b_law, lead_law, missed_law = best("suspended")
small = [k for k, v in ranges("published").items() if v["max_draws"] < 10]
windows = st["origin_april_upratings"]
all_under = all(v["switches_expected"] < v["switches_realised"] for v in ranges("published").values())
assert all(spike["year"] in windows[o] for o in missed_law)
```

The paper reports an expected value and a few paths, not the probability of any outcome. This appendix shows why. We scored `{python} words(len(ranges("published")))` ways of putting a range on the two statutory inputs, and the OBR forecast alone, against what followed `{python} words(len(origins))` OBR forecasts (the `{python} origins[0]` to the `{python} origins[-1]`): the forecasts with at least two earlier forecasts whose target years had all been published, which the method built on past forecast errors needs. Each method is fitted only on data dated before the forecast, using today's revised figures, and scored on the September CPI and May–July earnings for the `{python} words(H)` years after the forecast year, which set the April rises two to five years after it.

The scores are proper scoring rules [@gneiting2007]: the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) for the gap between the triple lock and the Burnham plan after those rises, in points of the pension; the energy score for the two series over the years together; and the variogram score [@scheuerer2015], which rewards getting the dependence between years right. Lower is better for each. We also record whether the realised gap fell inside each method's middle 80%, and how many changes of lead between CPI and earnings the method expected against how many happened.

How April 2022 is scored decides the result (@tbl-appendix). Scored on the published May–July 2021 earnings growth of `{python} rate(tr["published"]["april_2022_inputs"]["earnings"])`, `{python} "every method expected fewer changes of lead than happened, and " if all_under else ""`the best placed `{python} words(b_pub)` of `{python} words(len(origins))` realised gaps in its middle 80%. Scored with earnings equal to CPI (`{python} rate(tr["suspended"]["april_2022_inputs"]["cpi"])`) that April, as the law set it when the earnings leg was suspended, the best placed `{python} words(b_law)` of `{python} words(len(origins))`; the best-scoring of those (`{python} lower1(D.STATUTORY_LABELS[lead_law])`) missed the `{python} listing(missed_law)` forecasts, whose rises include April `{python} spike["year"]`, set by September CPI of `{python} rate(spike["cpi"])`. The method built on `{python} listing([lower1(D.STATUTORY_LABELS[k]) for k in small])` has only `{python} min(ranges("published")[k]["min_draws"] for k in small)`–`{python} max(ranges("published")[k]["max_draws"] for k in small)` paths at these forecasts, so its middle 80% is the full range of those paths. Neither treatment gives a reliable 80% range, so we report the expected saving, which the backtest of @sec-calibration tests for bias, and describe the spread across paths as scenarios.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-appendix
#| tbl-cap: "The forecast-distribution backtest over the chronological OBR forecasts, with April 2022 scored as published and as in law: CRPS of the gap after the rises (points of the pension); how many realised gaps fell inside the method's middle 80%; the energy score and the variogram score over the same series in different years; and changes of lead, predicted against actual. Lower scores are better."
pubm, lawm = block("published")["methods"], block("suspended")["methods"]
body = []
for k, label in D.STATUTORY_SHORT.items():
    a, l = pubm[k], lawm[k]
    point = k == "obr_point"
    body.append([label, num(a["burnham_2030_crps_pp"], 2), "n/a" if point else a["burnham_2030_inside"],
                 num(l["burnham_2030_crps_pp"], 2), "n/a" if point else l["burnham_2030_inside"],
                 num(a["energy"], 2), num(a["vs_serial"], 2), f'{num(a["switches_expected"], 1)} / {num(a["switches_realised"], 1)}'])
display(Markdown(md_table(["Method", "Gap CRPS, published", "Inside", "Gap CRPS, in law", "Inside",
                           "Energy, published", "Variogram, published", "Lead changes, published"], body)))
```
